query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In non‐equilibrium Mg-containing LWHEAs, the supersaturated solid‐solution microstructure initially traps Mg homogeneously, but upon exposure to corrosive environments or high‐temperature oxidation conditions, Mg diffuses out to form fine-scale, Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates. This phase transformation depletes Mg from the matrix, thereby altering the kinetics and chemistry of the protective oxide scale formation and ultimately changing both corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: A lightweight high-entropy alloy with density below 6 g/cm³ exhibiting a metastable, predominantly solid-solution microstructure with homogeneously distributed Mg.
generation.intervention: Exposure to controlled corrosive environments (e.g., chloride-containing salt spray) and/or high-temperature oxidation (e.g., 600–800°C) to induce microstructural evolution.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted under standardized corrosion and oxidation conditions (ambient for corrosion with specified salt concentrations; controlled high-temperature environments for oxidation) on alloys meeting the density constraint (<6 g/cm³).
generation.structural_mediator: Fine-scale, Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates that form either along grain boundaries or intra-granularly as a result of Mg diffusion from the solid-solution matrix.
generation.mechanism: The non-equilibrium microstructure drives a diffusion-mediated phase separation during exposure. As Mg segregates to form intermetallic precipitates, the remaining matrix becomes depleted in Mg, which changes its reactivity. This selective depletion and precipitate formation modify the subsequent development, composition, and protective nature of the oxide scale on the alloy surface, thereby impacting both corrosion pathways and oxidation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast, metastable baseline, the alloy that undergoes phase separation will exhibit a measurable decrease in Mg content within the matrix, the emergence of Mg-rich precipitates, and an altered oxide scale (e.g., differences in composition and morphology) that leads to either increased or decreased corrosion and oxidation performance relative to the baseline.
generation.baseline: The initial, as-cast metastable solid-solution state of the Mg-containing LWHEA with minimal phase separation and uniform Mg distribution.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys with densities below 6 g/cm³ under controlled environmental conditions; behaviors outside these conditions (different densities, non-standard test conditions) may not follow the same transformation pathway.
generation.uncertainty: The exact extent to which Mg depletion affects the kinetics of oxide scale formation and the resultant corrosion performance is not fully established. Variations in minor alloying elements and processing history could also influence the precipitate formation and subsequent functional properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one retaining the as-cast non-equilibrium metastable microstructure and the other subjected to a homogenizing thermal treatment to remove supersaturation. Expose both sets to identical corrosion (e.g., salt spray test) and high-temperature oxidation conditions. Characterize phase changes, Mg distribution, intermetallic precipitate formation, and surface oxide scale properties by sampling over time.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) for phase identification and microstructure analysis
Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) or wavelength dispersive spectroscopy (WDS) mapping for Mg distribution
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for oxide scale morphology
Electrochemical corrosion tests (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization) for corrosion rate measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If there is no significant difference in Mg distribution, precipitate formation, or oxide scale characteristics—and consequently in corrosion and oxidation performance—between the metastable and homogenized samples, then the hypothesis that the evolution of Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates mediates the changes in corrosion and oxidation behavior is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractIn this study, new high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which contain lightweight elements, namely Al and Ti, have been designed for intermediate temperature applications. Cr, Mo, and V were selected as the elements for the Al-Ti-containing HEAs by elemental screening using their binary phase diagrams. AlCrMoTi and AlCrMoTiV HEAs are confirmed as solid solutions with minor ordered B2 phases and have superb specific hardness when compared to that of commercial alloys. The present work demonstrates the desirable possibility for substitution of traditional materials that are applied at intermediate temperature to Al-Ti-containing lightweight HEAs.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, alloys design, lightweight alloys

Complex concentrated alloys (CCA) represent a new group of materials, with complex microstructures, comprising of a large number of elements []. CCAs extend the established limits of the high entropy alloys (HEAs) concept by allowing a smaller number of elements in the composition and in various proportions, that can deliver mixed structures containing solid solution and well dispersed intermetallic phases. CCAs generally have higher configurational entropy than conventional alloys and are capable of obtaining complex, disordered compositionally complex solid solution structures. CCAs are distinct from conventional alloys in that they are not based on a single major element and rather include several main elements, which allow a high degree of freedom in alloy compositions and properties. Their properties, such as high temperature resistance, corrosion resistance, workability, and low density, offer a remarkable advantage in the use of CCAs for various extreme conditions applications [,].
